extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, researchers and policy makers interested in the tobacco industry
extracted.subtask_description: A general-purpose encyclopedic article describing the tobacco industry: definitions, history, economic characteristics, major firms, regulatory and litigation context, public-health responses, and production statistics. It synthesizes factual and policy information rather than providing prescriptive guidance for a single procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: WHO definition of 'tobacco industry' and treaty expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, the 'tobacco industry' encompasses tobacco manufacturers, wholesale distributors and importers of tobacco products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WHO treaty (ratified by 181 member states) expects those states to implement public health policies with respect to tobacco control 'to protect present and future generations from the devastating health, social, environmental and economic consequences of tobacco consumption and exposure to tobacco smoke.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Global treaty restrictions on sale, advertising, shipment and taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: The WHO's Global Treaty on Tobacco Control places broad restrictions on the sale, advertising, shipment and taxation of tobacco products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countries that sign/ratify are expected to adopt policies across these domains as part of comprehensive tobacco-control efforts; the U.S. has signed but (as of the article) not ratified the treaty in the Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act — ban on characterizing flavors
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 907(a)(1)(A) of the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act bans the use of any constituent, additive, herb or spice that adds a 'characterizing flavor' to the tobacco product or smoke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim of this ban is to prevent children and teenagers from becoming addicted to cigarettes at a young age; the Act's flavor ban does not apply to menthol cigarettes, which were exempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence about youth flavor preference as policy rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy rationale cites studies showing 17-year-old smokers are three times as likely to use flavored cigarettes as smokers over the age of 25.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This empirical finding is used to justify restrictions on flavored tobacco products to reduce youth initiation; such evidence is explicitly referenced in regulatory explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising restrictions and regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments around the world are increasingly restricting tobacco advertising, citing health issues as the reason to reduce tobacco's appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions take multiple forms (bans, limits on placement, plain packaging in some jurisdictions) and have tightened over time in response to public-health concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavy taxation as tobacco-control policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tobacco is often heavily taxed to raise government revenue and to serve as an incentive for people not to smoke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tax policy is presented as both a fiscal measure and a public-health tool; price sensitivity and sales trends are used to evaluate tax impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation grounds and legal accountability standards
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. litigation alleged that tobacco causes cancer, that companies knew this, and deliberately understated the significance of their findings; internal memos were used as evidence of industry knowledge and misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal outcomes have included large cash settlements (e.g., Master Settlement Agreement-style outcomes), class action suits, and variable success rates over time. The article notes differences in litigation landscapes across countries and procedural limits (e.g., class certification issues) that shape legal accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of international litigation and jurisdictional differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawsuits against the tobacco industry are primarily restricted to the United States due to differences in legal systems; many firms treat ongoing U.S. lawsuits as a predictable cost of doing business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative legal context matters for evaluating prospects and remedies; settlements and judgments vary by jurisdiction and legal procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry tactics to influence policy and public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Major tobacco companies often try to shape tobacco-control policy from behind the scenes, working through third parties and front groups that can obscure their links to the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents historical and ongoing strategies (e.g., obfuscating truths, misleading advertising claims) that are relevant when assessing industry statements, partnerships, or self-regulatory claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-cigarette/ENDS market participation and regulatory scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Large tobacco companies have entered the electronic cigarette market (by acquisition or creating own products), and by 2014 all major multinationals had ENDS offerings; market concentration in transnational tobacco companies is noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health community is concerned about industry dominance in ENDS given historical misleading behavior; regulatory responses include premarket review/authorization pathways (e.g., FDA marketing authorizations) and litigation/settlement activity involving e-cigarette firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical role of product placement and regulation in entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Tobacco historically had a long relationship with the entertainment industry—cigarettes were deliberately placed in films and used for atmosphere—until health regulators tightened rules and anti-smoking pressure increased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This history explains part of tobacco's cultural influence and motivates contemporary restrictions on advertising and product placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tobacco as an agricultural commodity — economic/quality determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Tobacco is an agricultural commodity; its price is determined in part by crop yields, species/cultivar, quantity on market, geographic area of production, plant health, and product-quality characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic analyses of tobacco production should account for agronomic variability, species differences, and market supply conditions when evaluating production, pricing, and policy impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of production statistics (FAO/FAOSTAT) as a metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Unmanufactured tobacco production is tracked by organizations such as the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and reported as thousands of tonnes by country/region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These production figures are used to compare regional output, inform policy, and contextualize market shares and public-health interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry consolidation and market structure as evaluative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Following mergers, acquisitions and spinoffs, a small number of firms (Altria, British American Tobacco, Imperial, Japan Tobacco, Philip Morris International) dominate international markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market concentration affects regulatory strategy, political influence, and competition in new product markets (e.g., ENDS); assessing industry behavior requires attention to corporate structure and cross-border ownership.
